quote: Welche Beziehung besteht zwischen den Wurzeln dieser Gl und denen der Gl $f(x)=0$.?
english: What relation exists between the roots of this equation and those of the equation f(x)=0?
topic: Three short notes: questions on the discriminant of a quadratic form built from the roots of an algebraic equation (the equation with real roots in lambda), a question on directly proving regularity of solutions of differential equations other than Laplace's, and the problem of counting the possible configurations of n circles in the plane.

triage.modern_statement: Here is my best reading, which is partly a guess. Take a real polynomial f(x) with roots a_1,…,a_n. Build a symmetric quadratic form from those roots, for example a Hermite/Sylvester-type form Q(u)=Σ_i (u_0+u_1 a_i+…+u_{n-1}a_i^{n-1})^2. Its matrix is the Hankel matrix of the Newton power sums. The 'equation in λ with real roots' would then be the characteristic (secular) equation det(Q−λI)=0, whose roots are real because Q is symmetric. Hilbert asks how the roots λ_j (the eigenvalues of the form) relate to the roots a_i of f(x)=0. The page does not show exactly which form Hilbert built, so the question cannot be pinned down exactly.
triage.answered_by: No specific answer can be assigned. A related and well-known classical result is Hermite's and Sylvester's: the rank and signature of the Hermite form give the number of distinct roots and the number of real roots of f. That result concerns the signs of the eigenvalues, not an exact formula linking the λ_j to the a_i. I found no source that addresses this note or its exact question.

evidence.claim: The Hermite form, studied by Hermite for one-variable polynomials, is Tr(M_{fg}) = Σ_v mult(v) f(v) g(v). Its rank and signature count the complex roots and the real roots. This is a known link between the form built from the roots and the roots themselves.

triage.why: The note says 'this equation' without giving the form or the equation, so I can only reconstruct it as above. The matching classical theory is Hermite's root counting with quadratic forms (19th century). It answers the qualitative part through signature and real-root counting. In general there is no closed-form relation between the eigenvalues of the power-sum Hankel matrix and the roots of f. I found nothing tying this note to Hilbert's published problems or to any later work, and one search turned up only general material on the Hermite form.
